name: Zubair Sumayyah Ajike
missingPieces: D1 omits the cookie missing Secure/SameSite finding (substituted username enumeration); F3 hardcoded secret and F8 XXE lack the canonical evidence (the literal secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 and the 04-import-xxe.xml SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd payload). D2 has no file-read/open-redirect PoC hops and no scope-change-to-/api/v1/internal senior insight. D4 does not address the journalist prompt and omits NDPA section 41.
feedback: D1 is a strong, complete-looking catalogue: you caught all the heavy hitters with the right class and CWE and a quoted line, SQL injection at login.php:12-14 with the 02:15:31 302, unsalted MD5 as A02 CWE-916, JWT alg:none as A07 CWE-347 off Token 2, no-expiry CWE-613, stored XSS with the 185.220.101.9:8443 cookie beacon at 02:18:47, path traversal at 02:24:02 returning root:x:0:0, and open redirect via ?next. Two things held D1 back. Your XXE evidence is just a generic XML parse error rather than the actual 04-import-xxe.xml payload with SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd, and your hardcoded-secret finding never quotes the literal sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 or its line, so both read as guesses not proofs. You also dropped the cookie missing Secure and SameSite finding and used a username-enumeration entry in its place, which is defensible as an extra but is not one of the ten. On the decoy you did good honest work: you did not fall for labelling alg:none the decoy, and you correctly proved __DIR__ is a safe magic constant, but the intended safe construct was the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals for constant-time comparison, so I could give partial not full credit there. D2 traces the chain in the right order with the 02:14:55, 02:15:31, 02:16:04 and 02:18:47 stamps and verbatim payloads, and you stated your naira assumption openly, the per-customer mean times 312 giving roughly 70.9M, which is exactly the reasoning we wanted rather than a bare number. Where D2 lost ground: you have no PoC hop for the file read or the open redirect, and your CVSS vectors mark A:H almost everywhere including SQLi at 9.8, but the auth bypass does not touch availability, so SQLi should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, and most of your other A:H values are similarly inflated. You also missed the senior insight that a forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is the real scope-change story. D3 is the best part of this submission: the executive summary lands jargon-free on 312 customers and the naira figure, the threat model is concrete, findings are tied to captures, and crucially your remediation is ordered by effort and risk-reduction-per-hour with real hour estimates, not by raw CVSS, which is what we ask for. Your two detection stopgaps are also properly specified, the SQLi WAF rule on ARGS:username at 0.1 percent false positive and the alg:none SIEM alert at 0 percent, with exact fields. The one report blemish is citing GDPR for the breach clock when this is Nigerian data, so it should be the NDPA. D4 makes the right call and cites ISC2 Canon I and II by number as load-bearing and Section 40 of the NDPA tied to the 312 customers and the 72-hour NDPC clock, in your own voice anchored to your findings. It loses marks because you never answer the journalist prompt at all, and you omit Section 41, the duty to notify the affected data subjects on high risk, which matters precisely because 312 people are exposed. I looked for room to push this into the higher band and the missing cookie finding, the thin XXE and secret evidence, and the inflated A:H vectors genuinely cap it where it sits. The single most important fix: make every finding stand on quoted evidence and a correctly justified CVSS vector, starting with setting SQLi to A:N and quoting the actual XXE payload and the hardcoded secret string.
